**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership and the platform team
**From:** Infrastructure planning
**Re:** Recommendation on our next capacity decision

**Summary**

We are at a decision point on compute capacity. Our current cluster of eight GPUs is running hot during peak hours, batch jobs are queuing, and two recent product experiments were delayed because nobody could get a slot. The obvious instinct is to buy more hardware. My recommendation, after looking at the numbers and talking with the teams affected, is that we should not buy more hardware yet. We should first spend a focused six weeks improving utilisation of what we own, and hold the purchase decision at the end of that period with better data in hand.

**The case for buying, and why it's weaker than it looks**

The argument for new hardware is straightforward: demand is growing, our p95 queue times for training jobs have crept from minutes to hours, and latency-sensitive inference workloads occasionally degrade when a batch job hogs memory. Buying four more cards would make all of that go away, at least for a while.

But the purchase is expensive in more ways than the invoice. Capital cost is only the beginning. New cards mean new power and cooling headroom in a rack we're already close to the limit on, which likely means a facilities conversation and possibly an electrical upgrade. There's the ongoing operational burden: more devices to monitor, more failure domains, more driver and firmware churn. And there's a real opportunity cost. The same budget would fund roughly two engineer-quarters, and right now our binding constraint is not headcount but the reliability of the serving path — something hardware alone won't fix.

There's also a depreciation question we've been avoiding. Our current cards are two generations old. Buying more of the current generation now locks us into a refresh cycle that will collide with the next architecture jump, and resale value on used accelerators falls faster than our finance model assumes. Money spent today on hardware we may underutilise is money we can't spend in eighteen months when the right purchase is clearer.

**What better utilisation actually looks like**

The utilisation data tells a more hopeful story than the queue times suggest. Average GPU utilisation across the fleet sits around 45 percent, but peak-hour contention is real. That gap means our problem is partly scheduling, not raw capacity. Three concrete opportunities stand out, and I'll describe them in prose rather than pretend they're a checklist.

First, our inference serving is badly packed. Models are pinned to specific cards with generous memory reservations, so a card running a small model at 20 percent utilisation can't accept a second workload. Moving to a shared serving layer with proper memory partitioning could meaningfully raise effective density without touching hardware.

Second, batch and training jobs currently compete with latency-sensitive traffic with no priority classes. A simple preemption scheme — training jobs yield when inference demand rises — would eliminate most of the latency degradation we've seen, at the cost of slightly longer training wall-clocks, which almost nobody cares about.

Third, our overnight window is nearly idle. Shifting elastic jobs into it is mostly a scheduling policy change, not an engineering project.

None of this is glamorous, and none of it is free — it's maybe three to four engineer-weeks of real work, and there's a risk that the serving-layer refactor surfaces nastier problems than we expect. But it's work that pays off regardless of what we later decide about hardware, which is exactly what makes it a good first move.

**Reversibility and the option value of waiting**

This is the heart of my reasoning. Buying hardware is largely irreversible: once purchased, the money is spent, the rack space is consumed, and we own the maintenance burden whether or not demand materialises. Improving utilisation is reversible in the sense that it leaves every option open — if demand keeps growing, we buy in three months with better information, and the scheduling work still has value. Waiting costs us some schedule risk on experiments; buying costs us capital and flexibility. Given genuine uncertainty about whether recent demand is a step change or a spike tied to two specific projects, the option to defer is worth a lot.

**Uncertainty I want to name honestly**

I could be wrong about the demand curve. If the two delayed experiments turn into funded product lines, our utilisation gains will be absorbed within weeks and we'll need hardware anyway — and buying later may mean paying more or waiting on vendor lead times, which are currently long and getting longer. That's a real risk of the wait-and-see approach. To hedge it, I propose we qualify the purchase now: get quotes, confirm rack power headroom, and secure a procurement path, so that if the six-week review says buy, we can execute in days rather than months.

**Recommendation**

Fund the utilisation work now, treat it as a six-week experiment with explicit metrics (p95 queue time, peak-hour utilisation, inference latency under load), and revisit the purchase at the end with real numbers. Keep the procurement path warm in the meantime. We buy hardware when we know we need it, not when queue anxiety makes it feel urgent.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Engineering Lead
**Date:** This week's planning cycle
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?

We've reached the point in our AI roadmap where the question of capacity can no longer be deferred. Our inference workloads are bumping against the limits of the hardware we own, batch jobs are queuing overnight, and the team is spending real hours working around contention rather than building product. The instinctive response — buy more GPUs — deserves scrutiny, because I believe it is the wrong first move, though not for the reason people usually assume.

Start with the economics. Our current fleet sits at roughly 35–40% utilisation when measured across a full week. That number hides a lot: we have sharp peaks during business hours when interactive inference dominates, and long troughs overnight and on weekends when the machines mostly idle. Buying more hardware to cover the peaks means paying for silicon that will sit dark most of the time. At current prices, each additional accelerator carries not just its capital cost but power, cooling, rack space, and — the cost we consistently underestimate — the operational attention of keeping it healthy. We are a small team. Every node we add is a node someone has to patch, monitor, and troubleshoot at 2 a.m. when a driver hangs. The marginal cost of ownership is paid in our scarcest resource, which is engineering time.

Latency cuts both ways in this decision. More hardware would obviously relieve contention at peak, and for user-facing inference, tail latency is a product feature — p99 response times have crept up enough that I've heard from two downstream teams. But a large share of our latency problems trace to scheduling and batching behaviour, not raw capacity. Jobs land on whatever node is least loaded rather than the one best suited to them; interactive requests queue behind batch workloads that could run at 3 a.m.; our batching windows are tuned conservatively because nobody has had time to retune them since the model mix changed. If we fix utilisation first, we may find that the latency problem shrinks to something a modest purchase can actually solve, rather than something that demands a full expansion.

Reliability is the quieter argument. A larger fleet is, statistically, a more fragile fleet: more failure domains, more driver-version drift, more chances for a silent misconfiguration to corrupt results. Conversely, improving utilisation forces us to build the scheduling, monitoring, and queueing discipline that also makes the fleet more observable and more resilient. There is a real risk, though, that tighter utilisation means less headroom — a fleet run at 80% has no slack to absorb a node failure gracefully. Any efficiency push must preserve explicit reserve capacity for failover, or we will trade a cost problem for an availability problem, and availability problems are more expensive.

Then there is opportunity cost, which I want to weigh honestly. Every week spent building better scheduling and capacity tooling is a week not spent on the roadmap. That is a genuine sacrifice, and if our demand curve were steep and certain, I would say buy now and optimise later. But our demand is not certain. Two of the three workloads driving growth are experimental, and one may be replaced by a vendor API if the pricing negotiation lands where we expect. Buying hardware against uncertain demand is a bet; improving utilisation is closer to a hedge, because the tooling pays off under almost any demand scenario.

That points to the deepest consideration: reversibility. Hardware is the least reversible thing we buy. It depreciates, it locks us into a form factor and a vendor ecosystem, and unwinding a purchase means selling at a loss or letting it idle. Software and process changes — better queueing, smarter placement, time-shifting batch work, tightening our batching windows — are almost entirely reversible. If we invest three sprints in utilisation and discover demand genuinely outstripped our fleet, we will have lost little and learned a great deal about our true requirements, which will make the eventual purchase better targeted. If we buy first and demand disappoints, we are stuck with the bill.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next six weeks to a focused utilisation effort — placement improvements, batch scheduling, and honest measurement of where our latency actually comes from — while holding a pre-approved budget for a modest hardware expansion that we trigger only if utilisation exceeds 65% sustained for two weeks without latency recovery. I want to be clear about the uncertainty here: my utilisation figures come from coarse instrumentation, and it is possible that a deeper look reveals our peaks are irreducible, in which case buying becomes the right call quickly and we should not let the optimisation project become an excuse to defer a necessary purchase. If, in six weeks, the data says we're genuinely capacity-bound, we buy, and we'll do it with confidence rather than instinct.

Please come to Thursday's planning session with objections, especially from anyone who thinks the measurement period is a stall. I'd rather argue this out now than regret it in a purchase order.

— Engineering Lead
